activity: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
knowledge_domain: the idea that printed words carry meaning and that books are read front to back
fact: Your name written down has the same letters in the same order every time.
story:
Amelia went to the library with her mother. She wanted a book about a big red dog. She looked and looked. She found one at last.

She opened the book. The dog was on the first page. She turned the pages one by one. The story went on and on. Then she was at the last page. "It ended!" she said. "I read all the way to the end."

"Now you can take it home," said her mother. "But first we sign a card." Her mother wrote Amelia on the card. Amelia looked at it. The letters were A, m, e, l, i, a. Then she looked at her little red bag. Her name was on that too. A, m, e, l, i, a. Same letters. Same order. She put her finger on the card. She put her finger on the bag. "It's me, two times!" she said.

The librarian laughed. "Two Amelias," she said. Amelia gave the dog book a little wave. "Come on, book," she said. "Home time."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Matches and lighters are only for grown-ups to use.
story:
Scarlett was playing in the yard. She wanted to find a pretty stone for her pocket. She looked by the flowers. She looked under the bench. Then she saw something small and yellow. It was a lighter. It had rolled under the swing.

Scarlett bent down low. She looked at it. She did not pick it up. She knew it was not a toy.

"Mom!" she called. Mom came out slow and calm. "That is for grown-ups only," said Mom. Mom picked it up and put it high on a shelf. "Good job telling me," she said.

Scarlett went back to looking. She looked by the flowers again. At last she found a round white stone. It was warm from the sun. She put it in her pocket.

Later Scarlett felt tired. She took her stone to bed. She held it until her eyes closed.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Holding your nose closed makes food taste less strong.
story:
Aubrey sat at the dinner table. Her bowl was full of warm soup. "I don't want soup," she said. "It smells too strong." Her nose knew it. Her nose did not like it.

Mom sat down beside her. "Take a little sip," said Mom. "You are lucky. It is mild today." Aubrey looked at the soup with her eyes. She heard it go plop, plop in the bowl. She touched her spoon with her fingers. "One, two, three," she counted the carrots.

Aubrey had an idea. She held her nose closed. She sipped the soup. It tasted plain, like warm water. "Oh!" she said. She let go of her nose. She sipped again. Now it tasted strong again. Aubrey giggled. She held her nose. She let go. She held it again. "Pass the bread, please," she said. Mom passed the bread. Aubrey dipped it in the soup. Then she ate the whole bowl, spoon by spoon. "More soup, please," said Aubrey.

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Adding white paint to a colour makes it lighter.
story:
Livia went to the art gallery with Papa. She saw a big red circle on the wall. "Red," said Livia. Then she saw a big blue square. "Blue," said Livia. Papa smiled. There was a yellow star too. "Yellow!" said Livia. Her feet made a little noise on the shiny floor.

In the corner was a paint table for kids. Livia wanted to paint a sky. She stirred red and yellow together. Now she had orange! But her sky was dark blue. Too dark. Livia made a sad face. A boy next to her had white paint. "You can use some," he said. "Thank you," said Livia.

Livia dripped white into her blue. She stirred it round and round. Her dark blue got lighter. Now it looked like a soft morning sky. Livia held it up high. "Look, Papa! My sky!" she said. Papa clapped his hands, and the boy clapped too.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Wear a helmet when you ride a bike.
story:
Thomas stood in the bathroom. He wanted his bath now. He saw the big faucet. He reached up his hand.

Daddy caught his hand. "Not that tap," said Daddy. "That water is hot." Daddy turned the small tap instead. Cool water came out. Thomas put his fingers in. "Cold!" he said. Then Daddy added warm water, slow and careful. Thomas touched it. Warm now, like soup.

Thomas got in the tub. He splashed and played with his yellow duck. The duck went under. Then it popped up. Thomas laughed. Daddy washed his hair. The water ran down, drip drip.

Bath time was done. Daddy lifted Thomas out. The towel was soft on one side. The other side felt rough. The rough side dried his toes fast. Thomas got his pajamas on. Then he saw his cookie on the sink. He took a big bite. "Yum," he said.

Then Thomas heard a bell outside. His friend Mia was on her bike. Thomas ran for the door. He did not stop. He almost forgot something. Daddy held up the red helmet. Thomas ran back. Daddy put it on his head. It clicked under his chin. Thomas ran outside to his trike.

Mia rang her bell again. Thomas pushed his pedals. Off he went, helmet shining in the sun.

activity: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
knowledge_domain: to put on a coat and zip it up by themselves
fact: A coat helps keep your body warm when it is cold outside.
story:
Nora saw the snow out the window. Big brother Sam was going to the bus stop. Nora wanted to go too. She ran to the door with no coat.

Mom opened the door a tiny bit. Cold air came in. It went right down Nora's neck. "Brr!" said Nora. Her arms got little bumps. The wind was loud outside. Nora stepped back. "I need my coat," she said.

Her red coat was on the hook. Nora pushed one arm in. Then the other arm. The zipper was tricky. Up, up it went, all by itself. "I did it!" said Nora. Mom smiled. "My warm little sheep," said Mom. Nora pretended to be a sheep. She said, "Baa!" Then she held Sam's hand. They walked out into the snow, warm all over.

activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
knowledge_domain: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
fact: A grown-up plugs the charger into the wall.
story:
Miles went to the library with his dad. They rode the bus. The bus was big, and Miles held his dad's hand. At the library, Miles saw the tablets on a low table.

"I want to draw," said Miles. He pushed the round button. The screen lit up. Miles tapped the drawing app. A dog appeared! He tapped blue, and the dog turned blue. He tapped red, and the sky turned red. "My taps make it change," said Miles.

Then the tablet went dark. "Why did it stop?" Miles asked. "It needs power," said Dad. Miles found the charger on the shelf. It was heavy. He carried it to his dad, who plugged it into the wall. Miles waited. The screen lit up again. He drew one more blue dog, then put the tablet back on the table, all by himself.

"Hungry?" asked Dad, hanging up his coat. Miles smiled and said, "Yes, and I want the bus home."

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Everyone helps clean up the toys they played with.
story:
Cooper built a big tower of blocks. He made a long track for his cars too. Then he heard the rain stop. He ran to the window. The wet street was shiny in the sun.

"I want to go out," said Cooper. He started to run to the door. Dad held his hand. "The cars need a home first," said Dad. Cooper looked back. The blocks were all over the rug. The cars were everywhere.

Cooper went back. He put one block in the basket. Then another. He slid a car onto the shelf. His socks would slip on the rug, so he walked slow and careful. Soon the rug was clear. The room looked big and calm.

"Now we can go," said Dad. Cooper clapped his hands and held the door.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Saying how you feel, like "I feel sad," helps grown-ups know how to help you.
story:
Sara went to the library with Dad. She wanted the big bear book. She ran to the shelf.

A boy was there first. He held the bear book. Sara stomped her foot. She felt angry. She wanted to yell.

Then she saw the boy's face. A tear ran down. He looked sad. "I feel sad," the boy told the librarian. "The dog book is gone."

The librarian smiled. "Let's look together," she said. She found the dog book on a cart. The boy hugged it. He was happy now.

Sara felt excited. She waited for her turn. The boy gave her the bear book. "Thank you," she said.

On the way home, Sara told Dad, "I feel happy." Dad gave her a big hug. The bear book felt warm in her arms.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: After you sleep tonight and wake up, today will be called yesterday.
story:
Declan is at daycare. He paints a big sun. The paint is red and warm looking. It smells like paint, a little bit like crayons.

"My paint will not stick," says Declan. He tries to stick the paper on the wall. It falls down.

"That is the problem," says Miss Amy. "The paint is wet now. It will dry later. You can take your sun home tomorrow."

"Where does today go when I sleep?" asks Declan.

"It gets a new name," says Miss Amy. "Tomorrow we will call it yesterday."

Declan sleeps in his bed. The moon is out. In the morning the sun is out again.

At daycare, Miss Amy holds up his painting. It is dry now. The red sun looks different, shiny and smooth.

"You made this yesterday," she says.

"Yesterday I made the sun," says Declan. He hugs the paper to his chest.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Spread butter with the flat side of the knife, pushing it across the bread.
story:
Charlie stood on her stool by the counter. Mama put warm toast on her plate. The toast smelled so good.

"I want to do it myself," said Charlie. Mama gave her a dull knife with some soft butter on it. Charlie poked the toast with the pointy tip. The toast tore. Little bits fell off. "Oh no," said Charlie. "Why did it tear?"

She looked at the knife. It had a flat side too. What would the flat side do? Charlie turned the knife over. She pushed the flat side across the bread. The butter spread out thin and smooth. One push, two pushes, three pushes. The whole toast turned shiny.

"Now the milk," said Mama. Charlie took the small cup and the little pitcher. She poured very slowly. Drip, drip, drip. Would it spill? The milk went up, up, up. Not one drop fell.

Charlie took a bite of her toast. "I made it myself," she said. She looked at the flower on her cup. "Can I do it again tomorrow, Mama?"

activity: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
knowledge_domain: celebrating a birthday with family and friends
fact: If a cake has one candle for each year, a child turning five gets five candles.
story:
Madeline sat on a big chair at Grandma's house. Today was a party. It was Sam's birthday. Sam was turning five. Grandma brought out a chocolate cake. It smelled sweet like cocoa.

"Look at the candles," said Mom. Madeline looked. She pointed at them. She counted out loud. "One, two, three, four." Then she stopped. She looked at Sam. Sam held up his hand. His fingers were spread wide.

"There are four candles," said Madeline. Mom looked at the cake. Mom looked at Sam. Then Mom got another candle from the box. She pushed it gently into the frosting. Now Madeline counted again. "One, two, three, four, five." Five candles for five years.

The room felt warm and full of voices. Grandpa lit the candles with a long match. The little flames wiggled. Madeline stood far back and watched. The cake sat in the middle of the table, glowing. Everyone sang to Sam. Then Sam took a big breath.

"Make a wish," said Madeline. Sam blew out all five candles at once. Grandma cut the cake with a safe knife, far from small hands. She gave Madeline a cool slice on a blue plate. Madeline clapped and took a big bite.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: Steam from a pot or kettle is hot and can burn, so stay back.
story:
Maria put on her new hat. She ran to the backyard. Grandma was at the little grill with a pot. The pot went puff, puff, puff. Little white clouds rose up. Maria wanted to see the bubbles in the pot. "Come see," said Grandma. "Stand here by me."

Maria stood next to Grandma. The pot went puff, puff, puff again. Maria stepped back one step. The white clouds touched the air above her head. They did not touch Maria. Grandma stirred the pot. Round bubbles went blub, blub, blub.

"I see them!" said Maria. She watched from her spot by Grandma. Then she wiped the little table with a cloth. She set out cups, one, two, three. Grandma carried the pot over, slow and careful. They sat in the shade. "Hot tea for me," said Grandma. "Cold water for you." Maria drank her cold water. Her new hat kept the sun off. The pot sat far away, going puff, puff, puff.

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The word 'five' and the numeral 5 mean the same number.
story:
Alice went to the store with her brother. He was hungry for apples. "We need five apples," he said.

Alice held up her hand. She counted her fingers. "One, two, three, four, five," she said.

The apple bins had big signs. One sign had a 5 on it. Alice looked at the 5. Then she looked at her five fingers. "It is the same," she said. The 5 meant five apples!

Alice put apples in the bag. "One, two, three, four, five," she said. Her brother counted too.

At home, Mom washed the apples. Alice tried a small bite. It was sweet and crunchy. Her brother smiled and held up one apple. "One left for you," he said.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: In games like soccer and basketball, the team with more points at the end wins.
story:
Lydia went to the big stadium with Mom and Dad. The green field was far away. The crowd was loud. Lydia held her bunny tight.

The red team ran and ran. The blue team ran and ran too. "The red team ran the most," said Lydia. "Red wins!" Dad smiled. "Let's look at the board," he said. Lydia looked up high. The board said: red team, one point. Blue team, two points. "Blue has more points," said Lydia. "Blue wins!" The whistle blew. The blue team jumped and hugged. "They ran less, but they got more points," said Lydia.

Lydia skipped in a little circle. Her tummy felt giggly. Mom laughed. The blue fans waved their scarves. One fan, two fans, lots of fans. "Same team, same scarves," said Lydia. She waved her little blue scarf too. Dad lifted her up high. Lydia shouted with the crowd, "We won! We won!"

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Saying "sorry" is a way to show you know you hurt someone.
story:
Emilia went to the store with Mama. She wanted to pick a present for Grandma. There was a big basket of apples near the door. Emilia ran to see it. She bumped into a boy. His apple fell down and rolled under the shelf. The boy made a sad face. Emilia said, "Sorry." She got down on her knees. She reached into the deep, dark space under the shelf. Her hand came back with the apple. The boy smiled.

Then it was their turn at the apple basket. The man in front took one apple and stepped away. Emilia waited. She took one apple and put it in Mama's bag. The boy waited too. He took one apple. They each had one apple. It was fair.

At the toy shelf, Emilia found a soft red scarf. It would keep Grandma warm. She held it up to show Mama. The boy waved bye from the door. Emilia waved back and hugged the scarf tight.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: We feel things by touching them with our skin, like our fingertips.
story:
Chloe sat at the kitchen table. Mom put a plate in front of her. On it were a cracker, a lemon, and a soft bit of bread.

"Let's play a game," said Mom. "Find your five senses."

"Easy!" said Chloe. She pointed at her eyes. "I see with these. I see the cracker."

"Yes," said Mom. "What about the lemon?"

Chloe sniffed the lemon. Her nose wiggled. "I smell with my nose! It smells sour."

She bit the cracker. Crunch, crunch. "I hear it! My ears hear it. And my mouth tastes it."

"Now the bread," said Mom.

Chloe squeezed it. It was squishy. "I feel it with my hand!"

"With your skin," said Mom. "Your fingertips feel it."

Chloe touched the plate, the lemon, the bread again. Each one felt different. "My fingers know so much!"

She touched Mom's nose. "Your nose feels squishy too!"

Mom laughed. "Stop that, silly girl!"

Chloe sat back and held up her hand. "Five senses. I found them all!"

Then she touched her own nose. "Boop," said Chloe.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Pool steps or a ladder help you get in and out of the water.
story:
Andrew was at the lake with Dad. The lake had a little pool by the shore. Andrew wanted to swim in it. He held Dad's hand. He went down the steps, one step at a time. The water felt cool. "Kick, kick," said Dad. Andrew kicked. His feet made splashes. A shy fish swam away fast. Andrew laughed. "Again," he said. He kicked again and again. He was tired now. He wanted to get out.

Andrew pulled on the pool edge. It was too tall. He slipped back into the water. He tried again. Still too tall. Dad stood close by. "Look, Andrew," said Dad. "There are more steps." Andrew saw the steps. He held the rail. He went up, one step at a time. It was easy. He sat on the warm grass. "I did it," said Andrew. Dad clapped. Then Andrew yawned. "Nap time," said Dad. Andrew lay on the towel. His eyes closed. The water went pop, pop against the steps.

activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
knowledge_domain: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
fact: Milk goes back in the fridge after pouring, to keep it cold.
story:
Chloe wanted toast with butter, all by herself. Daddy made the toast. The toast was hot, so Daddy put it on her plate. Chloe held the little knife. She spread the butter. The butter made a mark on the toast. She pushed more, and the butter slid. Slip, slip, slip. Now the toast was all yellow. Daddy laughed. "Good spreading, Chloe!"

Next came the milk. Chloe held the cup with one hand. She poured slowly with the other hand. The milk went in the cup. Not one drop spilled. "I did it!" said Chloe. Then she ran to show Mama. On the way back, she saw the milk jug. It sat by the wall, far from the fridge. The milk needed to be cold. Chloe picked up the jug. She pushed the fridge door. She put the milk inside. The door shut with a little bump.

Outside the window the sky looked stormy and gray. "Rain soon," said Daddy. Chloe drank her milk. It was nice and cold. She took a big bite of toast. "Butter face!" said Daddy. Chloe giggled. There was butter on her nose.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: Taking slow, deep breaths can help you feel calmer when you are scared.
story:
Emilia sat in the big chair at the clinic. Today she would get a shot. Her tummy felt funny and her arms felt weak.

"Will it hurt a lot?" she asked Grandpa.

"Just a tiny pinch," Grandpa said. "Now smell this." He held up his jacket. It smelled like cookies. Emilia took one slow, deep smell. Then Grandpa counted, and she let the air out slow, like a birthday candle going out. Her tummy felt better. They did it again. And again.

The nurse came in with a little line of medicine in the tiny needle. Emilia took a slow, deep breath. She smelled the cookie smell. She blew it out slow. Then the nurse said, "All done!"

"That was it?" Emilia asked. She looked at her arm and smiled. "Can I have a sticker now?"

"You sure can," said the nurse, and she picked out a shiny gold star.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: It is hard to see in the dark, so we turn on a light.
story:
Henry ran to the park with his teddy bear. The sun was warm on his face. He heard kids laugh and shout. The swings went squeak, squeak!

Henry saw a big tunnel to crawl through. He held teddy tight. But inside the tunnel, it got dark. Henry could not see! He dropped teddy. Teddy was gone in the dark.

"Dad!" Henry called. "I can't see teddy!" Dad came fast. He took out his phone and made a light. Dad shone the light into the tunnel. Now Henry could see! There was teddy, right by his knee. Henry grabbed him and hugged him tight.

Then Henry smelled something smelly. "Pee-yew!" he said. It was his own shoe, full of sandbox sand. Dad laughed. "Let's talk about it at home," he said. "We can wash your feet."

On the walk home, they got an ice pop. Henry tasted the sweet orange ice. "Yum!" he said. He touched teddy's soft ear. Dad said, "See the big blue sky? It looks like the ocean!" Henry waved his hand at the sky. Then he took one more happy lick of his ice pop.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Later means some time after now, not right away.
story:
Henry went to the library today. Yesterday it had rained, so he could not go. Today the sun was out. "Can I play with the blocks?" Henry asked. The librarian smiled. "You can play later," she said. "First we will sing songs now."

Henry sat on the soft red rug. He clapped his hands. He sang about a little duck. The songs were fun, but he kept looking at the blocks. "Is it later yet?" he asked Mom. "Not yet," said Mom. "Sing one more song first."

Henry sang the last song. The singing stopped. Now his hands were quiet. Now the room was quiet. "Is it later now?" he asked. Mom nodded. "Yes. Now it is later."

Henry ran to the blocks. He stacked them up, up, up. He made a tall red tower. Then he pushed one block at the bottom. The whole tower fell down. All the blocks went bump on the rug. Henry laughed. "The little block made them all fall!" he said.

At home, Mom gave Henry a small cake. He got to lick the frosting off his fingers. "Can we go to the library again?" he asked. "Tomorrow," said Mom. Henry smiled. "Tomorrow is after today."

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Blocks, dolls and balls are all toys.
story:
Hayden ran to the big library playroom. He wanted the red ball, but it rolled far under the shelf. He got down on his knees. The ball was too far back. He could not reach it.

Then he saw a girl named Mia. She had a loose tooth that wiggled when she smiled. She was filling the toy box. "Blocks," she said, dropping them in. "Dolls," she said, and they went in too. Hayden watched. Then he had an idea. He found a long stuffed elephant. The elephant had a big gray trunk. He pushed the trunk under the shelf. He wiggled it like a magic wand. Out rolled the red ball!

"Good trick," said Mia. She clapped her hands. Hayden hugged the elephant and threw the ball high. It bounced, bounce, bounce, all the way to the story rug. "Again!" said Mia. Hayden ran after it.

activity: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
knowledge_domain: to count a group of up to ten objects and say which of two groups has more
fact: Zero means none, so an empty plate has zero cookies on it.
story:
Lincoln wore his blue coat to the corner store with Dad. On the counter sat a plate of little cookies. Ten cookies! Lincoln pointed at them one by one. "One, two, three," he said. He counted all the way to ten.

"I want two," said Lincoln. Dad said he could have two. Lincoln took one cookie and ate it. Crunch! He counted again. Nine cookies. He took another one. Munch, munch. Now eight cookies sat on the plate. "The plate has fewer now," Lincoln said. The man behind the counter smiled. "How many now?" he asked.

They counted together as the cookies went home with other people. Seven, then six, then five. Lincoln watched and waited. At last the plate was empty. "Where did the cookies go?" he asked. "How many are left?" Dad held up the plate. "Zero," said Lincoln. "Zero cookies. Zero means none!" The shy little store cat came out then. Lincoln laughed and held out his empty hand. "Zero cookies for you too, cat."

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: A blessing before a meal often says thank you for the food.
story:
Joshua sat at the big table in the hall. It was cloudy outside. His tummy made a little growl. "Soon," said Grandma. "First we say our blessing."

Grandma folded her hands. "Thank you for this food," she said. Everyone said it together. Then Joshua thought of something. "Who made the bread?" he asked.

"The baker did," said Grandma. "And a farmer grew the wheat."

Joshua put his hands together again. "Thank you, baker!" he said. "Thank you, farmer too!" The man at the desk by the door laughed a kind laugh. A dog outside went bark, bark, as if it wanted to say thank you too.

"Again, again!" said Joshua. So everyone said it one more time. Then the bread basket came around, and Joshua took the biggest piece. "I said two thank-yous," he whispered to Grandma. "So I get the big one." Grandma smiled and gave him a bit more.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'hello' when you meet someone is a friendly way to greet them.
story:
Anna ran to the playground. The sun made the slide shine like gold. A big lion spring toy waited there. It had a dark mane and a long tail. Anna wanted to ride it very much.

But a little boy sat on the lion already. He bounced up and down. He bounced very fast. Anna waved at him. The boy did not wave back. He jumped off and hid behind his grandma.

Anna thought and thought. "How can he be my friend?" she asked herself. "I can say hello." So Anna took one step. Then one more step. She peeked around the grandma's coat. "Hello," said Anna, in a small kind voice.

The boy peeked out. He looked at Anna. Then he smiled. "Hello," he said back. He came out from behind the coat. "Want to bounce too?" he asked. "Yes, please," said Anna.

They bounced on the lion together. Anna bounced so high she bumped the boy's arm. "Sorry," said Anna. The boy rubbed his arm. "It is okay," he said. Then Anna wanted to sit in front. "Can you help me?" she asked. The grandma lifted her up. "Thank you," said Anna. The two friends bounced and bounced, all the way to the pretend moon. "Roar," said the lion, in their big pretend voices.

activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
knowledge_domain: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
fact: Many Christian families say grace, a short prayer of thanks, before meals.
story:
William went to a big festival with his friend Sam. There was a playground with a red slide. William ran to it. He went down fast. His hat began to fall off. He caught it just in time.

Then it was time to eat. Sam's family sat at a long table. They all held hands. Sam's mom asked, "Would you like to say grace, William?"

William did not know what that meant. Sam whispered, "You say thank you for the food." William thought hard. He held hands tight, so no food would fall off the table.

"Thank you for the yummy bread," William said. Everyone smiled. Sam's dad cut the bread with a sharp knife. He gave William the first big piece.

"Can I say it again next time?" William asked.

"You sure can," said Sam.

activity: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
knowledge_domain: to name the five senses and say which body part is used for each
fact: Covering your ears with your hands makes sounds seem quieter.
story:
Blake walked on the nature trail with her mom. She wanted to learn her five senses. "Each one uses a body part," Mom said. Blake wanted to say them all by herself.

A big truck rumbled by. It was so loud. Blake put her hands over her ears. The sound got quieter. "That is neat!" she said. "My ears hear the truck. My hands make it quiet."

Mom smiled. "Yes, ears are for hearing." Blake looked around. "My eyes see that green leaf," she said. "My nose smells rain coming." She touched a smooth rock. "My hands feel this." Then she said, "My tongue tastes my snack!" They sat on a bench and Blake poured juice from her little cup. She sipped it and grinned. "Five senses, all by me," she said. "Now let's hear the birds."

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: The counting words always go in the same order: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten.
story:
Axel ran to the block corner at school. He wanted to build a big tower today. His friend Mia was already there. She was stacking blocks and counting them out loud.

"One, two, four," said Mia.

"Wait," said Axel. "Where did three go?"

Mia counted again. "One, two, four." The tower wobbled. Mia frowned. She wanted to count all ten blocks before the tower got too tall.

Axel thought hard. He sang the counting song in his head. He knew how it went. The numbers always came out the same way. "Try it like this," he said. "One, two, three. Then four comes after three!"

Mia nodded. She touched each block. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven." Then she stopped and laughed. "Eight! I almost forgot eight."

"Then nine," said Axel, bouncing on his toes. "And ten is last."

Together they counted the whole tower. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten!" The tower stood tall and thick like a wall of snow. It did not fall down.

"Ten blocks!" shouted Mia.

Ms. Rios clapped from across the room. Axel put one more block on top. The tower swayed. Then it came down with a crash. Blocks rolled everywhere. The two friends fell into giggles and began to count them again.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Families often gather together to celebrate special holidays.
story:
Michael ran up the steps to Grandma's house. The door swung open fast. "Happy day!" Grandma called. Inside, the house was full of people. Aunts, uncles, and cousins were everywhere.

Michael wanted to find his cousin Ben. He had not seen Ben in a long, long time. But the room was too crowded. Michael looked behind the big chair. No Ben. He looked by the table of food. No Ben. Then he heard a giggle from the hallway. Michael peeked around the corner. There was Ben, hugging a soft pet rabbit!

"Ben!" Michael shouted. Ben jumped up and they hugged tight. "Come see the candles," Ben said. The two boys sat with Grandma. Grandma lit the candles, one by one. Michael watched each little flame grow tall.

Later, Michael got sleepy on Grandma's lap. Ben leaned on his mom's shoulder. "Same time next holiday," Auntie whispered. Michael smiled. He closed his eyes and dreamed of rabbits.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Bennett jumped into the car seat. "We're going to Grandma's!" he called. Dad started the car. The big truck next to them rumbled away, fast. Their car went slow in the line.

Bennett looked out the window. The sun made his arm feel hot. Dad turned on the air. Now cool air blew on his face. "Better?" Dad asked. "Better!" said Bennett.

Then came the problem. Baby sister Mia began to cry. Her cry was loud. Very, very loud. Bennett wanted her to sleep. Grandma had a yummy cake waiting, and a plate with his name on it. But Mia would not close her eyes.

Bennett had an idea. He clapped his hands, loud, loud, loud. Mia cried louder. That did not work! So Bennett tried a tiny pat on his knee. Tap. Tap. Tap. It was so quiet. Mia blinked. Her cry got small. Then it got quiet too. Her eyes closed.

"She's sleeping," Bennett whispered. Dad smiled and drove on, down the big road, past the small houses, all the way to Grandma's cake.

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A grandparent is a parent of your mom or your dad.
story:
Grandma was coming to stay for a whole week. Violet waited in the kitchen. She tapped her toes on the floor. Then a car pulled up, and Grandma came in with a big bag. Grandma hugged Violet tight.

Violet had a worry. "Grandma," she said, "are you my mom's friend?" Mom was mixing cake batter at the counter. Grandma laughed a funny laugh. "Come and see," she said. She pointed at Mom. Then she pointed at herself. "I am Mom's mom." Violet looked at Mom. Mom nodded and smiled. Violet's eyes got big. Grandma was Mom's mom! So Grandma was a grandma to her.

"Can I paint you a picture?" Violet asked. Grandma sat down at the table. Violet painted a sheep with wiggly legs. Mom put the cake in the oven. Violet and Grandma waited side by side. "Warm cake for my girl," said Grandma, "and for my girl's girl too."

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: If you get lost in a store, tell a store worker you can't find your grown-up.
story:
Andrew ran to the big red slide. The sun felt warm on his face. The slide was warm too, from sitting in the sun all morning. He touched it with one finger first, then slid down fast. "Wheee!"

Next to the slide stood a bouncy pig. It was a pig on a spring. Andrew bounced on the pig. His boots went up and down. Near the pig, he saw a shiny bottle on the snowy ground. The snow crunched under his feet. He reached for it, but a big kid said, "Don't touch that. Ask a grown-up." Andrew put his hands in his pockets instead.

Then Mom said, "Let's get warm cocoa at the park store." Inside, Andrew looked at a wall of cookies. He turned around. Mom was not there. His tummy felt funny. He walked to the lady at the checkout. "I can't find my grown-up," he said. The lady smiled and called out, "Is a mom looking for Andrew?" Mom came around the shelf right away. She held his hand tight. The lady gave him a cocoa cup to hold with both hands. It was warm, not hot. Andrew took a little sip and smiled.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: Waiting in line means staying in your place until it is your turn.
story:
Blake went to the library with her dad. She found a new book about a duck on a lake. She wanted to take it home.

There was a line at the desk. Blake ran right to the front. A boy was already standing there. He held his book tight. "You have to wait," the boy said. Blake looked back. Three people stood behind him.

"Where is my spot?" Blake asked her dad. "At the end, by me," he said. Blake walked to the back of the line. She held her book. She waited.

The boy got his stamp and smiled. The next person went. Then the next. Soon it was Blake's turn. The librarian stamped her duck book. "You waited so nicely," she said.

On the way out, Blake waved to the boy. He waved back. "Can we read it tonight?" Blake asked. "Yes," said her dad. He took her hand, and they walked out into the sun.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: A day goes from morning, to afternoon, to evening, to night.
story:
Iris wants her red shoe. She cannot find it. She looked for it yesterday. She looked for it today. Now it is bedtime.

"Daddy, where is my red shoe?" she asks.

Daddy says, "Look in the morning. Now it is night."

Iris peeks out the window. The sky is dark. She sees the moon. "Night," she whispers.

She remembers her day. The sun came up. That was morning. Then she ate lunch. That was afternoon. Then Grandma came. That was evening. Then the sky went dark. That was night.

"Now I sleep," says Iris. "Later, the sun comes back. Then it is morning again."

She gets into bed. Daddy tucks her in. Her blanket is soft. It tickles her toes.

"Tomorrow you can look for your shoe," says Daddy.

"Tomorrow," says Iris. She closes her eyes.

In the morning, the sun peeks in. Iris lifts her blanket. She looks under the bed. There is her red shoe! A sticky candy wrapper is stuck to it.

Iris laughs. "Good morning, shoe," she says. She puts it on her foot.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: After painting, brushes get rinsed clean so the paint does not dry on them.
story:
Oliver was at summer camp. It was paint day. He sat at a big table with paper and brushes. He painted a lion. The lion had a yellow mane and a red tail.

After painting, the other kids rinsed their brushes in the water cups. Oliver wanted to paint more. He stuck his brush in the red paint cup. Then he ran outside to play.

The next day, camp was paint day again. Oliver grabbed his brush. He tried to paint a sun. The brush would not bend. It was hard like a stick.

"Is it broken?" Oliver asked.

"No," said his teacher, Maya. "Touch it. What does it feel like?"

Oliver touched it. It felt stiff and dry. The paint had dried on it.

Maya held out a new brush. "Here, you can share mine," she said.

Oliver painted a big blue sun. Maya helped him hold the brush flat. At the end, Oliver carried his brush to the sink. He rinsed it all by himself. The water turned pink. Then he shut off the faucet and set the brush on a paper towel.

The next morning, the brush was soft and bendy. Oliver smiled and painted a green lion with a purple mane.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: At storytime, a librarian reads books aloud to a group of children.
story:
Brielle stood by the little red chair. The reading corner had soft mats and a long shelf of books. She held her new library card in both hands.

"I want to take this one home," she said. It was a book about a sleepy bear.

But first she saw a boy by the rug. He stood at the edge of the storytime circle. He did not sit down. His toe tapped the mat, tap, tap.

The librarian sat down on her low chair. She held up a book with a pig on it. She opened it wide and read the first page in a big, happy voice. "This little pig found a big mud puddle!"

The boy laughed. Then he sat down on the rug with the other kids. Brielle sat down too, right next to him. The librarian read on. Her voice went high, then low. The pig got very muddy.

When storytime ended, the librarian helped Brielle scan her card. Beep! Then she scanned the bear book. Beep!

"You did it," the librarian said.

Brielle put the card in her pocket. She hugged the book all the way to the door.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: When people feel sad, they sometimes cry.
story:
Aiden ran to the park with his red truck. The sun did shine on the swings. Aiden felt happy. He pushed his truck up the ramp. The truck went far down the slide. That made Aiden laugh and feel excited.

Then Aiden heard a small sound. A girl sat by the sand box. Tears ran down her face. She was crying. Aiden felt sad just looking at her. He held his truck tight. He did not want to give it up. His tummy felt tight and a little angry too.

But the girl kept crying. Aiden walked over slowly. "Do you want my truck?" he asked. She wiped her eyes. She nodded. Aiden put the truck in her hands. She pushed it in the sand. Her tears stopped. She smiled a big smile.

Aiden felt warm inside. He sat down next to her. They made a road together. The truck went far, then came back. "Vroom," said the girl. "Vroom," said Aiden.

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: When you close your eyes, you cannot see the things around you.
story:
Matteo loved daycare days. Today Miss Ana said, "We will play hide and seek!" Matteo ran outside to the little hill. The grass felt soft under his hands. He touched it with his fingers.

"Where should I hide?" he asked himself. "Behind the short bush!" He could smell the flowers there. He could hear his friend Sam counting. He could see Sam's red shoes.

Then Matteo had an idea. He covered his eyes with his hands. Now he could not see the bush. He could not see Sam. He could not see anything at all. "Sam can't see me either!" he thought.

But Sam found him fast. "I saw you!" Sam laughed. "Your tummy was showing!"

Matteo tried again. He hid behind the hill. He kept his eyes open this time. He watched Sam look and look. Sam could not find him. Matteo waited and waited. The sun felt warm on his face. "The sun can burn your nose," Miss Ana had said, so he sat in the shade.

At snack time, Matteo ate a sweet apple. "Yum," he said. "My tongue likes this!"

"Matteo, where were you?" asked Sam.

"Behind the hill," said Matteo. "My eyes were open. That is why you could not find me!"

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin can be played by pulling a bow across its strings.
story:
One morning Beatrice went to Grandpa's house. She saw a big black case on the chair. "What is inside?" she asked. Grandpa smiled. "Open it and see." Inside was a little violin.

Grandpa gave her a stick with hairs on it. "This is the bow," he said. Beatrice took the bow. She poked the violin with the tip. The violin made a squeak. Beatrice laughed. Then she poked it again. Squeak, squeak, squeak. "That sounds funny," she said.

Grandpa sat close to her. He showed her how to hold the bow. Then he helped her pull it across the strings. The violin sang. It sang a long, sweet song. One pull, one song. Two pulls, two songs. Beatrice pulled the bow again and again. The music flew around the sleepy room like a bird.

Grandpa played too. He played fast, then slow. Beatrice moved her bow with him. "Can I make it soft?" she asked. "Pull it slow and soft," said Grandpa. So she did. The violin hummed like a small cat. Grandpa clapped his hands, and Beatrice took a little bow.
